My struggles are much more about losing focus, zoning out, and forgetting things rather than being impulsive.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced significant restlessness, fidgeting, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, which are issues that have been present since childhood?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really experience physical restlessness, fidgeting, or trouble staying still. Both now and when I was a child, my difficulties have always been more about mental drifting, daydreaming, and losing focus rather than being physically overactive.\n\nDoctor: Do you often forget important tasks, appointments, or deadlines, and do you have difficulty organizing your time and tasks effectively?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. I frequently miss dentist and vet appointments, pay credit cards late, and completely forget to reply to parent emails because they just fall off my radar. When it comes to organizing, I struggle to manage my time and end up bouncing between emails, half-finished outlines, and grading, which leads to last-minute scrambles to meet deadlines.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about your childhood, specifically if you had similar difficulties with focus, following through on tasks, or organization when you were in elementary school?\n\nPatient: Yes, these issues definitely go back to my childhood. In primary school, my teachers often wrote on my report cards that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, losing my homework, and forgetting instructions. My parents even had to sit with me every night just to get me to finish simple assignments because I kept spacing out.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant improvement in your focus and organizational abilities in quieter or more structured environments, such as during summer breaks or when working one-on-one with a student?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about it or tracked it that closely. The focus problems seem to be present most of the time, so I haven't noticed if quieter environments or one-on-one settings make a significant difference.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with starting and finishing tasks are more because you have trouble sustaining interest or motivation in the tasks, or because you genuinely can't seem to focus and stay on track, even when you're interested?\n\nPatient: It is definitely the latter—I start these projects with a lot of genuine interest and the best intentions, but I just can't seem to stay on track. Even when I try my hardest to focus, I quickly get sidetracked and find myself bouncing between emails, grading, and half-finished outlines instead of actually finishing what I started.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant symptoms of inattention or disorganization during periods of high interest or enjoyment, such as hobbies or activities you're passionate about?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure, as I haven't really thought about how it affects my personal hobbies. Most of my energy lately has been focused on how these struggles are impacting my teaching and causing tension with my wife at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you were engaged in a hobby or activity that you truly enjoy, and if so, did you still experience difficulties with sustaining focus or following through on related tasks?\n\nPatient: To be honest, I haven't really thought about that because I've been so consumed by my teaching workload and committee projects lately. I haven't had much time to engage in any hobbies, so I'm not really sure how my focus would be during them.\n\nDoctor: If you were to engage in a hobby or activity that you're truly passionate about, do you think you would still struggle with sustaining focus or completing related tasks, or would your interest in the activity help you stay on track?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure how I would do, to be honest. With all the work stress and extra responsibilities lately, I haven't had time for hobbies, so I haven't really thought about whether my interest would help me stay on track.\n\nDoctor: If you were to start a new hobby or project that you're extremely passionate about, do you think your difficulties with sustaining focus and completing tasks would still be present, or would your enthusiasm for the activity help you overcome these challenges?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure because I really haven't had any time for hobbies recently due to my work overload. However, even when I start school projects that I am genuinely excited about with good intentions, I still seem to struggle to follow through and finish them.\n\nDoctor: If you were fully engaged in an activity you're passionate about, such as a favorite hobby, do you think you could still focus and complete tasks related to it without getting distracted or losing track?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, as I just haven't had the time to test that out lately with my busy teaching schedule. I suspect I might still struggle though, because my focus issues seem to happen regardless of how much I care about what I'm doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or any other condition that might be contributing to your current symptoms?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been formally diagnosed or treated for ADHD or any other condition in the past. This is my very first time seeking a psychiatric evaluation, which I decided to do recently at the urging of my wife and department head, even though I can now see these issues have been with me since childhood.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel when you're unable to complete a task or project, such as feeling anxious, frustrated, or guilty, and how that affects your motivation to start new tasks?\n\nPatient: I haven't really analyzed those specific feelings or how they affect my motivation, to be honest. I just know that I always start my projects with the best intentions, but then I get completely overwhelmed trying to stay on top of everything.\n\nDoctor: When you're unable to complete a task or project, do you experience feelings of anxiety, frustration, or guilt, and if so, how do these emotions impact your motivation to start new tasks?\n\nPatient: I definitely feel stressed and overwhelmed by the backlog of unfinished work piling up on me. However, I haven't really analyzed whether I experience specific cycles of anxiety or guilt that block my motivation, as I usually still try to start new projects with good intentions.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on how the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed affect your motivation and ability to start new tasks, and whether this emotional response has been a consistent pattern throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Starting tasks actually isn't my main issue, as I usually begin projects with high motivation and very good intentions. The feeling of being overwhelmed and the struggle lie in sustaining my attention, staying on track, and actually finishing what I started. This pattern of struggling to follow through and complete tasks has been a consistent issue throughout my life, from childhood through university and my teaching career.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed by unfinished tasks contribute to your difficulty in sustaining focus, or are they a separate issue that arises after you've already struggled to complete tasks?\n\nPatient: I believe the stress and feeling overwhelmed are a result of my struggles, rather than the cause. These focus and follow-through difficulties are long-standing issues that go all the way back to my childhood, well before my recent work stress began. While the current stress certainly makes things much harder, it seems to arise from me constantly trying and failing to keep up with my workload.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations, either currently or in the past, where you might have exhibited more impulsive or hyperactive behaviors, even if they were not as prominent as your inattention symptoms?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any significant impulsive or hyperactive behaviors, either now or in the past. My struggles have always been much more about daydreaming, spacing out, and losing focus rather than being physically restless or acting on impulse.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you were able to focus and complete tasks without difficulty, such as during a highly structured or routine activity, and if so, what factors do you think contributed to your success in those situations?"

The feeling of being overwhelmed and the struggle lie in sustaining my attention, staying on track, and actually finishing what I started. It feels like I've always had to struggle to stay on track, regardless of the situation. When it comes to organizing, I struggle to manage my time and end up bouncing between emails, half-finished outlines, and grading, which leads to last-minute scrambles to meet deadlines.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about your childhood, specifically if you had similar difficulties with focus, following through on tasks, or organization when you were in elementary school?\n\nPatient: Yes, these issues definitely go back to my childhood. In primary school, my teachers often wrote on my report cards that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, losing my homework, and forgetting instructions. My parents even had to sit with me every night just to get me to finish simple assignments because I kept spacing out.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant improvement in your focus and organizational abilities in quieter or more structured environments, such as during summer breaks or when working one-on-one with a student?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about it or tracked it that closely. The focus problems seem to be present most of the time, so I haven't noticed if quieter environments or one-on-one settings make a significant difference.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with starting and finishing tasks are more because you have trouble sustaining interest or motivation in the tasks, or because you genuinely can't seem to focus and stay on track, even when you're interested?\n\nPatient: It is definitely the latter—I start these projects with a lot of genuine interest and the best intentions, but I just can't seem to stay on track. Even when I try my hardest to focus, I quickly get sidetracked and find myself bouncing between emails, grading, and half-finished outlines instead of actually finishing what I started.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant symptoms of inattention or disorganization during periods of high interest or enjoyment, such as hobbies or activities you're passionate about?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure, as I haven't really thought about how it affects my personal hobbies. Most of my energy lately has been focused on how these struggles are impacting my teaching and causing tension with my wife at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you were engaged in a hobby or activity that you truly enjoy, and if so, did you still experience difficulties with sustaining focus or following through on related tasks?\n\nPatient: To be honest, I haven't really thought about that because I've been so consumed by my teaching workload and committee projects lately. I haven't had much time to engage in any hobbies, so I'm not really sure how my focus would be during them.\n\nDoctor: If you were to engage in a hobby or activity that you're truly passionate about, do you think you would still struggle with sustaining focus or completing related tasks, or would your interest in the activity help you stay on track?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure how I would do, to be honest. With all the work stress and extra responsibilities lately, I haven't had time for hobbies, so I haven't really thought about whether my interest would help me stay on track.\n\nDoctor: If you were to start a new hobby or project that you're extremely passionate about, do you think your difficulties with sustaining focus and completing tasks would still be present, or would your enthusiasm for the activity help you overcome these challenges?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure because I really haven't had any time for hobbies recently due to my work overload. However, even when I start school projects that I am genuinely excited about with good intentions, I still seem to struggle to follow through and finish them.\n\nDoctor: If you were fully engaged in an activity you're passionate about, such as a favorite hobby, do you think you could still focus and complete tasks related to it without getting distracted or losing track?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, as I just haven't had the time to test that out lately with my busy teaching schedule. I suspect I might still struggle though, because my focus issues seem to happen regardless of how much I care about what I'm doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or any other condition that might be contributing to your current symptoms?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been formally diagnosed or treated for ADHD or any other condition in the past. This is my very first time seeking a psychiatric evaluation, which I decided to do recently at the urging of my wife and department head, even though I can now see these issues have been with me since childhood.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel when you're unable to complete a task or project, such as feeling anxious, frustrated, or guilty, and how that affects your motivation to start new tasks?\n\nPatient: I haven't really analyzed those specific feelings or how they affect my motivation, to be honest. I just know that I always start my projects with the best intentions, but then I get completely overwhelmed trying to stay on top of everything.\n\nDoctor: When you're unable to complete a task or project, do you experience feelings of anxiety, frustration, or guilt, and if so, how do these emotions impact your motivation to start new tasks?\n\nPatient: I definitely feel stressed and overwhelmed by the backlog of unfinished work piling up on me. However, I haven't really analyzed whether I experience specific cycles of anxiety or guilt that block my motivation, as I usually still try to start new projects with good intentions.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on how the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed affect your motivation and ability to start new tasks, and whether this emotional response has been a consistent pattern throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Starting tasks actually isn't my main issue, as I usually begin projects with high motivation and very good intentions. The feeling of being overwhelmed and the struggle lie in sustaining my attention, staying on track, and actually finishing what I started. This pattern of struggling to follow through and complete tasks has been a consistent issue throughout my life, from childhood through university and my teaching career.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed by unfinished tasks contribute to your difficulty in sustaining focus, or are they a separate issue that arises after you've already struggled to complete tasks?\n\nPatient: I believe the stress and feeling overwhelmed are a result of my struggles, rather than the cause. These focus and follow-through difficulties are long-standing issues that go all the way back to my childhood, well before my recent work stress began. While the current stress certainly makes things much harder, it seems to arise from me constantly trying and failing to keep up with my workload.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations, either currently or in the past, where you might have exhibited more impulsive or hyperactive behaviors, even if they were not as prominent as your inattention symptoms?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any significant impulsive or hyperactive behaviors, either now or in the past. My struggles have always been much more about daydreaming, spacing out, and losing focus rather than being physically restless or acting on impulse.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you were able to focus and complete tasks without difficulty, such as during a highly structured or routine activity, and if so, what factors do you think contributed to your success in those situations?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of any specific times where focusing has been easy or successful for me, even with routine tasks. It feels like I've always had to struggle to stay on track, regardless of the situation. I'm not sure what factors, if any, have ever really helped.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your main struggles are with sustaining focus and following through on tasks, but can you think of any situations where you might have felt restless, fidgety, or had an urge to get up and move around, even if it wasn't a major issue for you?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience physical restlessness, fidgetiness, or a strong urge to move around. My struggles have always felt much more mental—like my mind wandering, getting distracted, or zoning out—rather than any physical hyperactivity.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any notable differences in your ability to focus and complete tasks when you're working on something that has a very tight deadline versus when you have more flexible or open-ended timelines?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about comparing the two situations. However, regardless of how much time I initially had to work on something, I always seem to end up in a last-minute scramble to get it finished.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances where you successfully focused and completed a task without struggle, and if so, were there any specific factors or conditions that you believe contributed to your success in those instances?"
  }
]

I honestly can't think of any times where I was able to focus and finish a task easily without some level of struggle. It feels like I always have to put in an exhausting amount of effort to get anything done, or rely on last-minute panic to finally push me through.

The feeling of being overwhelmed and the struggle lie in sustaining my attention, staying on track, and actually finishing what I started. This pattern of struggling to follow through and complete tasks has been a consistent issue throughout my life, from childhood through university and my teaching career.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed by unfinished tasks contribute to your difficulty in sustaining focus, or are they a separate issue that arises after you've already struggled to complete tasks?\n\nPatient: I believe the stress and feeling overwhelmed are a result of my struggles, rather than the cause. My struggles have always felt much more mental—like my mind wandering, getting distracted, or zoning out—rather than any physical hyperactivity.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any notable differences in your ability to focus and complete tasks when you're working on something that has a very tight deadline versus when you have more flexible or open-ended timelines?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about comparing the two situations. I haven't had much time to engage in any hobbies, so I'm not really sure how my focus would be during them.\n\nDoctor: If you were to engage in a hobby or activity that you're truly passionate about, do you think you would still struggle with sustaining focus or completing related tasks, or would your interest in the activity help you stay on track?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure how I would do, to be honest. With all the work stress and extra responsibilities lately, I haven't had time for hobbies, so I haven't really thought about whether my interest would help me stay on track.\n\nDoctor: If you were to start a new hobby or project that you're extremely passionate about, do you think your difficulties with sustaining focus and completing tasks would still be present, or would your enthusiasm for the activity help you overcome these challenges?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure because I really haven't had any time for hobbies recently due to my work overload. However, even when I start school projects that I am genuinely excited about with good intentions, I still seem to struggle to follow through and finish them.\n\nDoctor: If you were fully engaged in an activity you're passionate about, such as a favorite hobby, do you think you could still focus and complete tasks related to it without getting distracted or losing track?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, as I just haven't had the time to test that out lately with my busy teaching schedule. I suspect I might still struggle though, because my focus issues seem to happen regardless of how much I care about what I'm doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or any other condition that might be contributing to your current symptoms?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been formally diagnosed or treated for ADHD or any other condition in the past. This is my very first time seeking a psychiatric evaluation, which I decided to do recently at the urging of my wife and department head, even though I can now see these issues have been with me since childhood.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel when you're unable to complete a task or project, such as feeling anxious, frustrated, or guilty, and how that affects your motivation to start new tasks?\n\nPatient: I haven't really analyzed those specific feelings or how they affect my motivation, to be honest. I just know that I always start my projects with the best intentions, but then I get completely overwhelmed trying to stay on top of everything.\n\nDoctor: When you're unable to complete a task or project, do you experience feelings of anxiety, frustration, or guilt, and if so, how do these emotions impact your motivation to start new tasks?\n\nPatient: I definitely feel stressed and overwhelmed by the backlog of unfinished work piling up on me. However, I haven't really analyzed whether I experience specific cycles of anxiety or guilt that block my motivation, as I usually still try to start new projects with good intentions.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on how the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed affect your motivation and ability to start new tasks, and whether this emotional response has been a consistent pattern throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Starting tasks actually isn't my main issue, as I usually begin projects with high motivation and very good intentions. The feeling of being overwhelmed and the struggle lie in sustaining my attention, staying on track, and actually finishing what I started. This pattern of struggling to follow through and complete tasks has been a consistent issue throughout my life, from childhood through university and my teaching career.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the stress and feeling of being overwhelmed by unfinished tasks contribute to your difficulty in sustaining focus, or are they a separate issue that arises after you've already struggled to complete tasks?\n\nPatient: I believe the stress and feeling overwhelmed are a result of my struggles, rather than the cause. These focus and follow-through difficulties are long-standing issues that go all the way back to my childhood, well before my recent work stress began. While the current stress certainly makes things much harder, it seems to arise from me constantly trying and failing to keep up with my workload.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations, either currently or in the past, where you might have exhibited more impulsive or hyperactive behaviors, even if they were not as prominent as your inattention symptoms?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any significant impulsive or hyperactive behaviors, either now or in the past. My struggles have always been much more about daydreaming, spacing out, and losing focus rather than being physically restless or acting on impulse.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you were able to focus and complete tasks without difficulty, such as during a highly structured or routine activity, and if so, what factors do you think contributed to your success in those situations?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of any specific times where focusing has been easy or successful for me, even with routine tasks. It feels like I've always had to struggle to stay on track, regardless of the situation. I'm not sure what factors, if any, have ever really helped.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your main struggles are with sustaining focus and following through on tasks, but can you think of any situations where you might have felt restless, fidgety, or had an urge to get up and move around, even if it wasn't a major issue for you?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience physical restlessness, fidgetiness, or a strong urge to move around. My struggles have always felt much more mental—like my mind wandering, getting distracted, or zoning out—rather than any physical hyperactivity.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any notable differences in your ability to focus and complete tasks when you're working on something that has a very tight deadline versus when you have more flexible or open-ended timelines?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about comparing the two situations. Even when I am genuinely interested in a project, I still find myself getting easily distracted and struggling to follow through.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare how often you forget important tasks or appointments versus how often you get distracted from tasks you're currently working on, to help me understand which of these issues might be more prominent for you?\n\nPatient: Getting distracted while actively working is a constant, daily battle; even when I block off time for curriculum drafts, I immediately end up bouncing between emails, half-finished outlines, and grading. Forgetting appointments or parent emails happens regularly too, but it feels less hourly than the struggle to stay focused on a task right in front of me. While both are incredibly disruptive, that day-to-day distraction feels like the more constant, uphill struggle.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you experience significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to your difficulties with focus, organization, and task completion, versus how often you simply struggle with these tasks but manage to cope without significant distress?\n\nPatient: Historically, I struggled but always found a way to cope and get by. However, over the last 11 months with my new school responsibilities, it has become a constant, daily source of significant distress. It has completely overwhelmed my ability to manage, leading directly to a critical performance review at work and ongoing tension at home with my wife.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the percentage of tasks or projects that you start but fail to complete due to your difficulties with sustaining focus and following through?"
